questions.text:
Read the following passage:

'The morning light crept through the curtains like a thief, stealing away the darkness that had comforted her through the night. She lay still, unwilling to face what the day would bring.'

The phrase 'crept through the curtains like a thief' uses a simile. Which choice BEST explains its EFFECT on the reader?
options: It makes the morning sound peaceful and welcoming
It suggests the morning is unwelcome and intrusive — the comparison to a thief implies the light is stealing something the character valued (the safety of darkness)
It is a literal description of someone breaking into the room
It tells us the curtains are very thick
questions.expectedAnswer: It suggests the morning is unwelcome and intrusive — the comparison to a thief implies the light is stealing something the character valued (the safety of darkness)
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer focuses on the EFFECT of the simile.

Here's why:
A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as'. Comparing morning light to a thief gives it a sneaky, unwelcome feel.
It also suggests the light is taking something away that the character wanted to keep — the comforting darkness. This sets up the character's reluctance to face the day.
Exam tip: in Year 10, identifying the technique is only half the answer — you must also explain WHAT EFFECT it has on the reader.

questions.text: In the same passage, 'darkness that had comforted her through the night' uses personification. Explain WHAT this personification suggests about the character's STATE OF MIND.
options: She is frightened of the dark
She finds the night more comforting than the day, suggesting she is dreading what the day will bring or escaping from something difficult in waking life
questions.expectedAnswer: She finds the night more comforting than the day, suggesting she is dreading what the day will bring or escaping from something difficult in waking life
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer infers the character's state of mind from the personification.

Here's why:
Darkness can't really comfort anyone — that's what makes it personification (a non-human thing acting like a human).
Giving the darkness this comforting role suggests the character WANTS to stay hidden in it, which implies she is avoiding something in the daylight.
This is reinforced by the next sentence ('unwilling to face what the day would bring').
Exam tip: every language feature is a CLUE to character or theme — link the technique to the bigger picture.

questions.text: What MOOD does the writer create in the passage about the morning light? Identify the mood AND explain HOW it is created using TWO specific words or phrases from the text as evidence.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark for clearly identifying the mood with appropriate words (reluctant, melancholy, anxious, uneasy, foreboding, gloomy).

1 mark for using TWO specific words or phrases from the text AND explaining how each contributes to that mood.

Examples of strong evidence:

'crept through the curtains like a thief' — the sneaky verb 'crept' and the negative comparison to a thief make the morning feel unwelcome and threatening.

'unwilling to face what the day would bring' — the word 'unwilling' shows reluctance and 'what the day would bring' implies dread of the unknown, building anxiety.

'darkness that had comforted her' — implies the character feels safer hiding from reality.

Do NOT award the second mark unless TWO pieces of evidence are quoted and explained.

questions.text:
Read this sentence:

'The ancient pohutukawa stood sentinel on the cliff edge, its gnarled branches reaching toward the sea like arthritic fingers.'

The writer's main PURPOSE in this description is most likely to:
options: Make the reader feel afraid of the tree
Build a vivid sense of an old, weather-beaten tree that has stood for generations as a guardian of the coast — connecting the natural world to the idea of age and endurance
Persuade the reader to visit the beach
Show that the tree is dying and needs to be removed
questions.expectedAnswer: Build a vivid sense of an old, weather-beaten tree that has stood for generations as a guardian of the coast — connecting the natural world to the idea of age and endurance
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer focuses on the LAYERED purpose.

Here's why:
The personification 'stood sentinel' makes the tree feel like a guardian — old, watchful, protective.
The simile 'like arthritic fingers' adds the idea of great age and weathering.
Together they don't just describe — they make the reader feel the tree's history and endurance.
Exam tip: at merit level, the writer's purpose is rarely just 'to describe' — it almost always carries an attitude or theme.

questions.text:
Identify TWO different language features in the pohutukawa sentence. For EACH feature you must:
• name the feature accurately
• quote the exact words from the text
• explain the effect on the reader (not just what it means).
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark per feature IF the answer includes name + quote + effect. 2 features required.

Examples of strong answers:

Personification — 'stood sentinel'. Effect: gives the tree a human role as a guard or watcher, suggesting it has stood watch over the coast for generations and creating a sense of protection and longevity.

Simile — 'like arthritic fingers'. Effect: by comparing the branches to twisted, pained fingers, the writer suggests great age, endurance and even discomfort — the reader pictures the gnarled, weathered shape and feels the weight of years on the tree.

Adjective choice / imagery — 'ancient', 'gnarled', 'cliff edge'. Effect: builds an image of harshness and time, placing the tree in a wild, exposed setting.

Do NOT award the mark for naming a feature without explaining its effect.

questions.text:
Read this extract from a persuasive speech:

'Every single day, 80 tonnes of plastic waste enters our oceans. That's the weight of 10 school buses. Every. Single. Day. Are we really going to sit here and do nothing?'

Which language feature is NOT used in this extract?
options: Repetition (with deliberate sentence fragments for emphasis)
Direct quotation from a named expert
questions.expectedAnswer: Direct quotation from a named expert
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is 'Direct quotation from a named expert'.

Here's why:
The extract uses a rhetorical question ('Are we really going to sit here...?'), repetition with fragments ('Every. Single. Day.') and a statistic ('80 tonnes').
It does not, however, name an expert or quote any source — there is no expert opinion.
Exam tip: persuasive writing usually uses several techniques together — be ready to spot which one is missing.

questions.text:
Explain HOW the writer of the persuasive speech tries to convince the audience to take action. In your answer:
• identify TWO different persuasive techniques (do not just list them)
• quote a specific phrase for each
• explain in detail HOW each technique works on the reader.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark per technique IF the answer includes name + quote + explanation of effect on the reader. 2 techniques required.

Examples of strong answers:

Statistics + comparison — '80 tonnes of plastic... the weight of 10 school buses'. Effect: the statistic feels real and shocking, and converting it to something familiar (school buses) makes a huge number easy for the audience to picture and feel emotionally.

Repetition with fragments — 'Every. Single. Day.' Effect: the deliberate full stops force the reader to slow down on each word, creating a hammering rhythm that makes the problem feel unrelenting and impossible to ignore.

Rhetorical question — 'Are we really going to sit here and do nothing?' Effect: it forces the audience to imagine themselves answering, and the wording assumes anyone honest would have to say 'no' — pushing them towards action.

Do NOT award full marks for naming techniques without quoting and explaining.

questions.text:
Read the following poem:

'Homesick

I carry my homeland
in the creases of my palms,
in the way my tongue curls
around vowels
my classmates can't pronounce.

I am two places at once —
here, where the rain falls sideways
and the hills are impossibly green,
and there, where the sun bakes
the red earth into memory.'

In an extended response (about a paragraph), explain how the poet explores the experience of living between two cultures. Your answer must:
• identify TWO specific language features (e.g. metaphor, contrast, sensory imagery) and quote them
• explain how each feature shows the speaker's identity and feelings
• explain how the CONTRAST between the two places adds to the meaning of the poem
• include ONE inference (something the poem implies but does not say directly).
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks total — award by tracking the four bullet points.

1 mark — identifies TWO specific language features with QUOTES. Examples:

Metaphor — 'I carry my homeland / in the creases of my palms' — homeland is part of the speaker's physical body.

Sensory/physical imagery — 'the way my tongue curls / around vowels / my classmates can't pronounce'.

Contrast — 'here, where the rain falls sideways' vs 'there, where the sun bakes the red earth'.

Metaphor — 'I am two places at once'.

1 mark — explains how each feature shows the speaker's identity and feelings (e.g. carrying homeland in the body suggests it can never be put down; the unpronounceable vowels show the speaker's language marks them as 'other' to classmates).

1 mark — discusses how the CONTRAST between the two places (cold sideways rain and impossibly green hills vs hot sun and red earth) shows the speaker is split between two real, vivid worlds — and that 'memory' suggests one of them now exists only in their mind.

1 mark — includes a clear INFERENCE the poem implies but does not state, e.g. 'the speaker is a recent migrant who feels neither fully part of NZ nor fully able to return home'; 'the poem implies a sense of loss — the home country has become a memory'; 'the speaker feels lonely in their NZ classroom but proud of their identity'.

Excellence answers will weave techniques, contrast and inference together into a single coherent analysis, not list them separately.
